MagDesk: Interactive Tabletop Workspace Based on Passive Magnetic Tracking

What it is

The paper's story: where it is used, its core idea and the real system demo.
Real-world use

A desk that tracks magnets in the objects above it

Imagine an office desk where a pen or a dial works with no battery, no wire and no camera.

the authors' demo · a dashboard worked with the magnetic stylus

It shows The authors' own demo: a stylus with a magnet in its tip works buttons and sliders drawn on a plain desk, with no wire.

How to read it Watch the stylus touch a widget on the desk; the screen at the lower right shows the same widget change.

drag to turn the space
Office · Open-plan desks · Sensing World ›
Motivation

Tracking objects on a desk in 3D

  1. The ability to precisely track objects in real-time expands the interaction space
  2. require a direct line-of-sight (LoS) between the tracked device and sensors or markers
  3. the estimated position accumulates errors over time
  4. GaussSense and its subsequent works instrument the backside of touchscreen displays with an analog Hall-sensor grid
  5. an alternative tracking modality is desired that is accurate, stable, and requires minimum instrumentation
what a camera sees

It shows A camera's view of the desk while a hand closes round the tracked object: its marker disappears, so the tracking stops.

How to read it The marker's dot is the tracked place; when the hand covers it, the dot is lost.

an IMU's position, against the truth

It shows An IMU adds up its small errors: its position estimate walks away from where the object really is.

How to read it Time runs to the right; dashed is the true position, solid the IMU's estimate, the gap growing.

a Hall grid's reading, by the magnet's height

It shows A Hall grid behind a screen sees the magnet only close up: past about 50 mm its image fades into nothing.

How to read it Height runs to the right; the bar is how bright the magnet's spot is, the grey band the 50 mm limit.

State of the art

Passive magnets were tracked close to the sensors only

  1. 1challenges associated with passive magnetic approaches, including achieving long-range capabilities and system scalability
  2. 2Compared with prior works that explored 3D tracking of permanent magnets, MagDesk provides a longer range
  3. 3MagDesk uses a novel approach to dynamically adjust the position and number of magnetometers used

It shows How high earlier magnet trackers could track: the 3-D ones in the paper's Fig. 6 stop near 300 mm, a Hall grid at 50 mm.

How to read it Each bar is one system, as the paper reports it; up is how high above the sensors it tracks a magnet.

Background

Four terms used throughout

Magnetometer01

112 low-cost magnetometers (MLX90393) underneath the surface

Magnetic dipole02

The field around a magnet can be modeled by the dipole model

Pose: 5 degrees of freedom (DoF)03

the 5-DoF pose of a spherical magnet is characterized by the parameters [x, y, z, θ, φ]

x, y, z: where it is; θ, φ: where its pole points.

Background field04

collects the background magnetic field at each sensor for 10 seconds without the magnetic objects

the field each sensor reads

It shows A round magnet's field lines and the arrow each sensor reads: the pattern shows where the magnet is and where its pole points.

How to read it Grey loops are field lines from north to south; each red arrow is one sensor's reading, longer where the field is stronger.

Core idea

The sensors' readings pin down the magnet's pose

  1. 1MagDesk combines the 3-axis sensor readings from an array of N magnetometers
  2. 2generates an optimal magnet pose that minimizes the differences between the readings and the dipole model
  3. 3the solver uses the pose in the previous cycle as the seed point
readings against the model

It shows Each sensor's reading beside what the dipole model predicts for the solver's guess: as the guess improves, the two agree.

How to read it Each bar is a sensor, dark measured and light predicted, with the mismatch below falling at each step of the search.

Core idea · what to observe

Each sensor reads the magnet's field, strongest beneath it

MagDesk tracks the movements of permanent magnets by sensing the spatial distribution of the induced magnetic flux density near the table surface

  1. The arrows: the field each sensor reads
  2. Strongest right under the magnet, fading fast to the sides
  3. The solver's pose follows the magnet, frame by frame
  4. Your turn Drag the magnet

Challenge 1 · weak field at height

The field fades with the cube of the distance

the tracking performance deteriorates when the magnet is higher, as the field of a dipole degrades with the cube of the distanceWorse, §3.1 warns the solver “might converge to an incorrect local minimum” and the tracking “would be lost”, since each frame starts from the last answer.

  1. The magnet rises
  2. Twice as far: an eighth of the field
  3. The noise stays: the pose scatters
  4. Solver alone: 3 mm near the desk, 100+ mm at 600 mm
  5. Your turn Raise the magnet
Height –
Field under it –
Solver's error –
solver's error by height

It shows The solver's error grows with height: a few millimetres near the desk, over 100 mm at 600 mm, as in the paper.

How to read it Dots: Fig. 6a's unfiltered errors; line: the model's, a still magnet at each height; ring: the error now, at the magnet's height.

Solution 1 · Kalman filter

The Kalman filter

The measurement noise of the Kalman filter is updated based on the estimated average tracking errorBefore use, a still magnet's error is measured every 5 cm of height. Each frame, the error expected at the solver's height tells the filter how noisy the new pose is. A short moving average follows it (Solution 2).

  1. New: a Kalman filter smooths the pose
  2. Its noise: the error expected here
  3. High up, a new pose counts less
  4. Filtered: about half the error, on averageFig. 6a, filtered: 2.49 mm near the desk and 60.92 mm at 600 mm. Mitigated, not solved: high up, centimetres are left.
  5. Your turn Switch it off, then raise the magnet

Challenge 2 · lag when fast

Averaging lags behind a fast magnet

the delay resulting from the moving average would degrade tracking performance when the magnet moves fastAveraging many poses helps a slow magnet: the paper notes poses “could be averaged over a longer time frame” when it moves slowly (§3.3.3). A fast magnet has moved on by then.

  1. New: the magnet runs round the paper's test path
  2. A fixed half-second average smooths the noise away
  3. Faster, and the average trails behind the magnet
  4. At 500 mm/s the trail is centimetres long
  5. Your turn Drag the magnet fast, then slow
Speed –
Error now –
test path, from above

It shows With a fixed half-second average, the estimate trails behind the magnet, more the faster it moves round the path.

How to read it Dashed: Fig. 5a's test path, its points 1 to 5 in red; dot: the magnet; gold: the estimate's last seconds; red line: the lag.

Solution 2 · adaptive window

A window set by speed

the window size of the averaging filter is updated based on the estimated magnet speed and average measurement errorThe speed comes from the last 0.6 s of the path. The window is the expected error divided by the speed: a slow magnet is averaged over more frames, a fast one over fewer, never over more than 0.5 s.

  1. New: the window follows the speed
  2. Slow: it grows, never past 0.5 s
  3. Fast: it shrinks, the estimate keeps up
  4. At 500 mm/s a little lag is leftTable 1: at 500 mm/s the error across the 600 mm range averages 36.53 mm, 153.7% more than a still magnet; the filter still takes 11.8% off. Mitigated, not solved.
  5. Your turn Turn it off; change the speed

Challenge 3 · two magnets close

Two close magnets can be taken for one

the magnetic field distributions surrounding the magnets overlap and disturb each other when two magnets are in close proximityCloser than the 100 mm between sensors, the paper says the solver “has a higher chance of identifying the two magnets as one” (§4.3.3).

  1. New: a second 5/8 in magnet
  2. Each solver reads sensors within 300 mm
  3. Under about 400 mm apart, each feels the other's field
  4. Near 80 mm apart, the error peaks
  5. Your turn Drag the second magnet closer
Separation –
Error now –
error by separation, Fig. 9

It shows One-magnet solvers get worse within about 400 mm, and worst near 80 mm, where both can take the two magnets for one.

How to read it Line: Fig. 9; gold dots: the model; ring: now; dashed: 400 mm; an arrow at the top: over 80 mm.

Solution 3 · two-magnet solver

A two-magnet solver

This alternative solver accepts the poses from both magnets as seed points and predicts two sets of 5-DoF position and orientation informationSeed points: the poses the search starts from, here each magnet's pose one frame before. 5-DoF: a pose's five numbers, x, y, z and the pole's two angles. So it fits ten numbers at once, both magnets, to every sensor.

  1. New: one fit for both magnets
  2. It reads the whole array
  3. Paper, 5/8 in, 30 mm apart: about 11 mmTwo 5/8 in magnets moved within 100 mm of the desk: 11.18 mm and 2.54° at 30 mm apart, about 7 mm far apart (Fig. 9). Mitigated, not solved. The model's magnets move slower, and its error is lower.
  4. Combined: switches below 400 mm (5/8 in)
  5. Your turn Pick a solver, then drag

Drawing with the stylus and the ink button

Goal: draw; the toggle button turns the ink onMagDesk tracks both magnets, the stylus's 3/4 in one and the button's 5/8 in one. The ink is on while it reads the button more than 10 mm down. Pressed fully and turned past 30°, the toggle button locks there (Fig. 11 b-3); turned back, it springs up.

Check the Paper · 2 of 3

Ablation study

Question Which part of MagDesk's pipeline keeps its error low?Ours: the paper tests the whole filter against the solver alone (Fig. 6, a still 3/4 in magnet) and two magnets moved at random (Fig. 9). Here, one magnet loops 5 to 45 cm up; or two sit near the surface, one swinging past the other.

You change
MagDesk's parts: one off at a time
  1. 1Your turn PressThe Kalman filter and the moving average both off: the solver's own poses are given, as in Fig. 6's unfiltered curve. The loop is ours: the 3/4 in magnet, 14 s a turn.
  2. 2Your turn PressOurs, not a test of the paper's. The measurement noise is how much the Kalman filter trusts each new pose; here it and the 0.5 s window stay one value at every height and speed.
  3. 3Your turn PressTwo 5/8 in magnets near the surface. Each has its own solver on the sensors within 300 mm of it, even when the two are close (Fig. 9's solid lines).
  4. 4Your turn PressEvery part on, two magnets: the combined solver uses the two-magnet solver while they are under 400 mm apart (Table 3).

Both runs hear the same move and the same sensor noise.To compensate for inaccurate prediction when the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) between measured magnetic fields and sensor noise is low, MagDesk implements a filtering pipeline on top of the analytical solver a fixed set of parameters for the Kalman and averaging filter is suboptimal as the expected prediction error varies with tracking heights, magnet sizes, and estimated speeds The maximum position error peaks at around 80 mm separation, which roughly corresponds to the 100 mm spacing between adjacent magnetometers The solver achieves average positional and orientational accuracy of 11.18 mm and 2.54 deg, respectively, even if the two magnets are as close as 30 mm apart MagDesk adopts an adaptive filtering pipeline a combined solver was implemented that automatically switches between the two types of solvers when a threshold distance is crossed

GaussSense's image is ours: its grid's field by our dipole model, its threshold set at the 50 mm its range ends at (§2.3).Compared with prior works that explored 3D tracking of permanent magnets, MagDesk provides a longer sensing range and higher tracking accuracy its tracking capabilities are limited to near-surface (within 50mm of the display) the tracking resolution is fundamentally limited by the sensor density, making extending up to desk or room-scale unrealistic

Go Beyond the Paper · 1 of 3

Generalization study

Question Where does MagDesk stop tracking: above 600 mm, or past the array's edge?The paper tests each size up to its range over the array (Table 2: 450 to 700 mm). Here the magnet goes higher, and past the sensors, which end 75 cm from the desk's centre.

You change
where the magnet is, and its size
  1. 1Your turn Raise it to 700 mm.Up there the 3/4 in magnet's field at the sensors nears their noise (§3.1): the solver's poses scatter, and the filter can only average so much.
  2. 2Your turn Move it past the edge.The sensors end 75 cm from the desk's centre; the top goes on to 87.5 cm. Past the edge they see the magnet from one side only.
  3. 3Your turn Pick the 1 in magnet.A larger magnet has a larger moment (9.01 against 3.80 A·m², Table 6): its field stays above the noise higher up.
    Magnet
  4. 4Your turn Back in range.300 mm over the desk's centre: inside every size's range.

Physical conditions

Question What changes MagDesk's error: noisier sensors, a faster sensor setting, or a drifting background?Each tab changes one thing the paper fixes, the others held at the paper's. The magnet moves to and fro 300 mm up; its handle raises it.

You change
the sensor noise, the sensor's setting, the background
Sensor noiseSensor's rateBackground drift
  1. 1Your turn Raise the noise to 2 µT.The paper does not give the MLX90393's noise. The model's 1.1 µT is fitted to Fig. 6a's unfiltered curve. Near the surface the field is far above it.
Error, last 4 s –
Solver alone –
Noise set –

What you saw SNR: the signal-to-noise ratio, how far the magnet's field at the sensors is above their noise. The filter reads its expected error from a table of errors by height, measured beforehand; it is scaled with the noise.The same magnet incurs a larger error at higher heights above the table as the SNR decreases

  1. 1Your turn Pick the fastest rate.One MLX90393 runs up to 716.9 Hz with more noise (§6.1.2). The paper gives no array rate at that setting: the model keeps the desk read every 31.2 ms and makes each reading 4.7× noisier (both assumed).

What you saw A what-if of the noise alone: the paper names 716.9 Hz for future work, a faster rate near the table surface (§6.1.2), and tests none.MagDesk’s current implementation uses a 32.1 Hz sampling rate to optimize for lower measurement noise and higher tracking accuracy

  1. 1Your turn Let the background drift by 5 µT.The calibration takes away the background read for 10 s with no magnet (§3.3.1). A change after it stays in the readings; the model takes it the same at every sensor.

What you saw The curve is a still magnet over the desk's centre. The magnet's own field falls with the cube of its distance, so a fixed offset matters most at height.while the Earth’s magnetic field is relatively stable, minor natural fluctuations do occur on the time scales of days and weeks, and thus, periodic calibration is needed

Go Beyond the Paper · 3 of 3

Optimal array setup design

Question How many magnetometers, and how far apart, does MagDesk need?The paper tests its array of 112 and two subsets, 32 and 18 sensors (§4.3.4). Here any number from 1 to 160 goes anywhere on the desk.

You change
where the magnetometers are, how many, and how deep
  1. 1Your turn PressThe paper's sparsest array: 18 sensors 300 mm apart (§4.3.4, Fig. 10), about 1 a square foot against 9 (Table 4). Here every third one each way: the paper does not say which.
  2. 2Your turn Raise the magnetFig. 10: a sparser array loses accuracy sooner as the magnet rises, and its range falls from 600 mm to 500 mm (Table 4). The grip above the magnet raises it too.
  3. 3Your turn Drag a magnetometer off the desk, or add someA magnetometer dragged off the desk is taken away; the slider adds one where the gap is widest. Each change runs the chain again on the new set.
  4. 4Your turn PressThe paper's own array: 16 × 7 magnetometers, 10 cm apart (§3.2), 3 cm under the top (Fig. 3).
